parts.title: Meeting an astronaut
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last month, our school had an unusual visitor: a real astronaut. Her name was Commander Joanna Reid, and she had spent five months on the International Space Station. Everyone in the school hall was silent when she walked on stage.

She began by showing us a short film of life in space. We saw her floating in the air and drinking water from a bubble. When she turned upside down, the whole hall laughed. Then she explained that the hardest thing was not the danger but the loneliness. 'I missed my family,' she told us, 'and I missed the smell of rain.'

After the talk, we were allowed to ask questions. A little boy in the front asked what astronauts eat for breakfast, and she answered that she had often eaten porridge from a bag. My friend Anil asked whether she was ever afraid, and she said that she was most afraid before the launch, not during it.

At the end, she told us that anyone could work for a space agency, not only brilliant scientists. 'You need patience and teamwork,' she said. I went home thinking about it all evening, and I have already decided to study physics.

questions.explanation: It showed her floating and drinking water from a bubble in space.

questions.explanation: She said the hardest thing was the loneliness.

parts.title: A short history of space travel
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
People have always looked up at the sky and wondered what was out there. [1] The first rocket to leave the Earth's atmosphere was launched in 1944, but nobody travelled in it.

The first person in space was Yuri Gagarin, a Russian pilot, who orbited the Earth in 1961. [2] The whole journey lasted only one hour and forty-eight minutes, but it changed history.

Eight years later, in July 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon. [3] About six hundred million people watched on television as he stepped onto the grey dust.

Since then, scientists have sent machines to Mars, Jupiter and even beyond the solar system. [4] Today, astronauts live on a space station for months at a time, and companies are planning holidays in space. [5] Some people believe that one day humans will live on other planets.
sentences: Armstrong later became a university professor.
His landing was shown live all over the world.
Their names are known to children all over the world.
Some of these machines are still sending pictures today.
A dog was the first animal to orbit the Earth.
Many dreamed of travelling there, but it took until the twentieth century to do it.
Ideas like these once seemed like science fiction.
He was only twenty-seven years old.

gaps.explanation: "Travelling there" and "the twentieth century" lead to the first rocket in 1944.
His age is extra information about Gagarin before the length of the journey.
"Shown live" explains why millions of people watched on television.
"These machines" refers to the machines sent to other planets.
"Ideas like these" refers to space holidays, which once seemed like science fiction.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Wolfgang, what time does the planetarium show finish? The website says half past five.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s the old timetable, I think. It was longer in the summer.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: So what is it now?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I phoned them yesterday. The show starts at a quarter past four and lasts forty-five minutes.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Oh, good. Then we have time for a coffee afterwards.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Yes, and we can still be home before dinner.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Great. Shall I buy the tickets online?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Yes, please. Two adults. I’ll bring my brother, he says he has never seen a planetarium before.

question.explanation: Half past five is the old summer timetable; the show starts at a quarter past four and lasts forty-five minutes, so it ends at five.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Hello, one ticket for the evening show, please. How much is it?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Adults pay twenty pounds. Children are twelve.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Oh, I’m a student. I’ve got my card here.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Then you get four pounds off. Let me check. Yes, that works.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Great. I nearly brought my daughter, but she has a test tomorrow.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: What a pity. Do you want a programme as well?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, thanks. I have to save my money for the bus home, and for a sandwich before the show.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: No problem. Enjoy the show.

question.prompt: How much will the man pay for his ticket?
question.explanation: Twenty is the adult price and twelve is the children’s price; as a student he gets four pounds off the adult price.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Good evening, and now the weather for stargazers. Many of you hope for a clear sky all evening long, but I’m afraid that won’t happen. The clouds will stay over the region for most of the night. We thought they would move away before dinner, but they are slower than we expected. The wind will arrive later and push them to the sea, so the sky will be open after midnight. If you can stay up, you will see the stars very well. Tomorrow evening will be cloudy again, so tonight is your only chance this week.

question.prompt: When will the sky be clear?
question.explanation: The clouds will not go before dinner or leave soon; the wind will clear the sky after midnight.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I want to see the Moon properly. Do I need a camera with a lens?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Not at all. I thought I would need one, and I asked in a shop, but they cost hundreds of pounds.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So can I just look up with my eyes?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You can see the Moon like that, of course, but you won’t see the craters. A pair of binoculars is plenty, and they’re cheap. I borrowed my dad’s.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Are they heavy?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: A bit, so rest your arms on a wall or a gate.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Great idea. I’ll ask my uncle if he has some.

question.prompt: What is enough to see the Moon?
question.explanation: A lens is too expensive and eyes alone do not show craters; she says binoculars are plenty.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Some people ask me if I’d live on Mars. My brother says no because it would be too hot, but he’s wrong, it’s very cold up there. My cousin says that rockets are scary, and he’s right, I suppose, but I’ve tried a simulator and I wasn’t afraid at all. The real reason is simple. I’d miss my room, my dog and my friends so much. Maybe I could visit for a week, but my home is here, on Earth, and I wouldn’t change it for anything.

question.prompt: Why wouldn't the girl live on Mars?
question.explanation: It is cold, not hot, and she is not afraid of rockets; she would miss her room, her dog and her friends.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Hi Ptolemy, it’s Hester. About tonight. I booked a table at Luigi’s, but they phoned me this morning and said they have a leak in the kitchen, so they’re closed. Then I thought about the museum, but it closes at five and we won’t finish work until six. So I’ve decided we should stay in. I found a new film about the planets, and I’ll make some pasta. Come at seven and bring a bottle of juice. See you later!

question.explanation: The restaurant has a leak and the museum closes early; they will stay in to watch a film about the planets.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Lionel, how long does it take to fly to the Moon?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I read that it’s about a week.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s for the small probes that use very little fuel. The first astronauts needed more than three days. I think it was three, yes.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: And four days?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s the time for the cheaper route that some new companies plan. But the journey that people have really done is the one I said, just a little more than that.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s faster than I thought. Like a long weekend.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Exactly.

question.prompt: How long does a rocket need to reach the Moon?
question.explanation: The small probes take a week and the cheaper route four days; the astronauts took three days.

parts.title: A night at the observatory
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: hadrian
turns.text: Good evening, everybody, and welcome to Hilltop Observatory. Tonight we are open from eight until eleven o’clock. Normally we close at ten, but because it is a special night with many visitors, we will stay open an hour longer. Please speak quietly, and switch off your phones, because the light of a screen makes it hard for everyone to see the sky. You may use the small red torches that we give you at the door. Now, what will you see? Many people hope to start with Saturn, and you will see it later, at about ten, when it is higher in the sky. But first, we will look at the Moon, because it is bright and easy, and it helps your eyes get used to the dark. Our telescope here is a big one. The mirror inside is thirty centimetres wide. The telescope in our other building has a mirror of sixty centimetres, but it is only for scientists. Ours can show you the rings of Saturn clearly. Because many people are waiting, each person can look for two minutes. I know it is short, and I am sorry. Last year we gave five minutes, but the queue was too long. If you want to look again, you can join the end of the queue. While you wait, please visit our café. It is in the room next to the entrance. A cup of tea is two pounds, but I recommend the hot chocolate, which is one pound fifty. Finally, please do not touch the telescope, and do not use flash photography. If you have any questions, please ask one of our guides in the green jackets, who will be happy to help you. Have a wonderful evening.

gaps.prompt: The observatory is open until ___ o'clock tonight
gaps.explanation: Normally they close at ten, but tonight they stay open an hour longer.

gaps.prompt: Visitors must turn off their ___ so that screens do not shine
gaps.explanation: Phones must be switched off; red torches are allowed.

gaps.prompt: The first object that visitors will look at is the ___
gaps.explanation: Saturn comes later, at about ten; first they look at the Moon.

gaps.prompt: The mirror in tonight's telescope measures ___ centimetres across
gaps.explanation: The telescope in the other building has sixty, but this mirror is thirty.

gaps.prompt: Visitors have ___ minutes each at the telescope
gaps.explanation: Last year they gave five minutes, but this year it is two.

gaps.prompt: The price of a hot chocolate is ___ pound fifty
gaps.explanation: Tea is two pounds; the hot chocolate is one pound fifty.

parts.title: A young astronomer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: Kavya, how did you become interested in space?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: A lot of people think it was a film, and I did love science fiction, but it only made me laugh. The planetarium was a school trip, and I fell asleep! No, it started when my uncle gave me a small telescope for my tenth birthday. The first night, I looked at the Moon, and I couldn’t believe how close it seemed. I’ve never stopped since.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: What’s the hardest part of your work?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: People assume it’s the maths, and yes, there’s a lot of it, but I enjoy it. Travelling to other countries to use the big telescopes is exciting, not hard. What’s really difficult is working through the night. Telescopes need dark skies, so I work from ten until six, and then I can’t sleep in the daytime. It took me years to get used to it.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: What do you do on most days?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Not what you imagine. I don’t build instruments, that’s the engineers’ job, and I only teach one class each term. Most days I sit at a computer and study pictures from telescopes, looking for tiny changes in the light of a star. It’s like detective work, and I really love it, even when nothing happens for weeks.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: Why do you like Saturn best?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Mars is popular, and I like the Moon, but Saturn is special. It’s not the first planet I ever saw, that was Jupiter, and it isn’t the biggest one. But even after ten years, when I look at the rings, my breath stops for a second. They look unreal, like a painting.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: What advice do you give to young people?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: Some say, study only physics, but you need other subjects too, like English, to write about your work. Others say, buy an expensive telescope. Please don’t. Just go outside and look at the sky every night. After one month you’ll know the stars better than most of your friends.

turns.speaker: rosalind
turns.text: How do you feel about your future work?

turns.speaker: kavya
turns.text: I’m excited. I want to find new worlds around other stars, maybe some like ours. Some days I’m tired of looking at pictures, I admit, but never tired of the job. I was afraid when I left my last job, but that’s over. I’d love to fly into space, but I’d rather stay here, and I may write a book one day, later, when I am a little older and have more time.
